outcome: OpenAI announced on 10 July 2026 that its GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra model had produced a proof of the cycle double cover conjecture; the proof and an accompanying Lean 4 formalization were released, independent expository write-ups by Jim Geelen and Sang-il Oum followed, and a guest post on The Matroid Union by Johannes Carmesin explicitly endorses the proof's correctness after reviewing multiple independent Lean formalizations and the expository accounts.

disputes.summary: The proof as formalized in Lean covers finite loopless bridgeless multigraphs (allowing parallel edges), which is a broader class than the traditional statement in terms of simple graphs; a commentator (toknow.ai) flagged that mathematicians must independently confirm the Lean definitions match the conventional conjecture's meaning before treating the formal check as settling the classical statement. This is a scope/definitional caveat rather than a rival proof or priority dispute.

summary: On 10 July 2026 OpenAI announced that GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra had produced a two-to-three-page proof of the cycle double cover conjecture (Szekeres 1973 / Seymour 1979) in under an hour using 64 subagents, releasing the proof PDF, the prompt used, and a Lean 4 formalization (github.com/openai/cdc-lean) that OpenAI reports builds cleanly with no 'sorry'/'admit' placeholders and no project-specific axioms. The proof reduces to cubic 3-edge-connected (multi)graphs, uses the Jaeger–Kilpatrick eight-flow theorem / a nowhere-zero F2^3-flow, and a linear-algebra duality argument to build an 8-cycle double cover (the stronger 5-cycle double cover conjecture remains open). Independent human expositions followed within days: Jim Geelen's arXiv note (2607.15399, submitted 16 July 2026, explicitly 'offers no new insights' but recasts the argument) and Sang-il Oum's arXiv exposition (2607.16356, submitted 17 July, revised through 1 August, v3 adding material on the small cycle double cover conjecture and matroid implications). Decisively, Johannes Carmesin — a graph/matroid theorist publishing in JCTB — wrote a guest post on The Matroid Union (21 July 2026) stating directly 'yes, the proof is correct,' after reviewing the argument's structure, the independent Lean 4 formalizations (by Krystal Guo's team, Carmesin's own team, and OpenAI's), and the Geelen/Oum expositions. This is the kind of expert digestion §6.1 treats as sufficient for `resolved` even absent journal publication, which as of my research (September 2026) has not yet occurred. TheoremDB lists the mathematical claim as 'Supported' citing these same expositions, though it separately notes it has not yet run OpenAI's Lean repository inside its own controlled verifier (a note about TheoremDB's own re-verification pipeline, not a doubt raised by any mathematician). The live Wikipedia article on cycle double cover has already been updated to describe the July 2026 preprint and its claimed resolution. Given a specialist's public, reasoned endorsement of correctness in a recognized expert venue, multiple independently-authored Lean formalizations, and no gap, retraction, or dissenting expert view found anywhere in my search, I classify this as `resolved` rather than `claimed`, while noting the caveat about journal non-publication and the multigraph-vs-simple-graph scope point in `competing_reading`.
competing_reading: A stricter reading would keep this at `claimed`: there is no refereed journal publication as of September 2026, Geelen's own note is explicitly not a verification ('no new insights'), and the toknow.ai piece raises a real definitional-scope question (multigraphs vs. simple graphs) that no source shows was formally closed. If Carmesin's blog post is read as a personal opinion rather than the kind of considered, venue-backed expert digestion §6.1 requires, or if The Matroid Union is judged not to rise to the level of a refereed check, `claimed` is the more conservative and defensible call. I weighed this and went with `resolved` because Carmesin's statement is unequivocal, made in a recognized subject-expert venue, backed by his own review of multiple independent formalizations, and unrebutted by any subsequent source I found.
what_would_settle_it: A journal acceptance, or an explicit statement from a second independent expert (beyond Carmesin) confirming the multigraph-vs-simple-graph formalization gap is immaterial or resolved, would remove the remaining ambiguity.
